analysis.investment_thesis: Chambal Fertilisers is a rare cheap-and-good combination: earnings yield of ~13.7% (EBIT INR 2,501 Cr / EV ~INR 18,199 Cr) clears my 12% hurdle, while ROCE of 26.8% signals a genuinely high-return business. With debt essentially eliminated (borrowings down from INR 10,113 Cr in FY20 to INR 99 Cr in FY25), the balance sheet is fortress-like and the stock trades at P/E of 9.5x.
key_strengths: Magic Formula metrics both pass: Earnings Yield ~13.7% and ROCE 26.8% — rare combination in Indian markets
Debt elimination is extraordinary: net debt went from ~INR 10,000 Cr (FY20) to net cash (-INR 9 Cr) in 5 years, entirely through operating cash generation
EBIT has been consistently in the INR 1,800–2,500 Cr band for 6 consecutive years — sustainable, not a one-time spike
key_risks: Fertiliser pricing is subject to government intervention (subsidy policy, urea price controls) — EBIT can be clipped by regulatory fiat
Revenue is highly volatile (INR 27,773 Cr in FY23 vs INR 16,646 Cr in FY25) due to commodity input prices (natural gas) and import parity shifts
CWIP jumped to INR 1,135 Cr in FY25 (from INR 184 Cr in FY24) — a large expansion in progress whose returns are unproven
red_flags: FCF dropped to INR 824 Cr in FY25 vs INR 2,718 Cr in FY24 as capex accelerated — monitor whether ROIC on new capacity holds up
Revenue concentration in urea (a subsidised product) creates dependence on Indian government subsidy disbursement timelines
analysis.detailed_analysis: Chambal hits both Magic Formula triggers convincingly. EV is only ~INR 18,200 Cr (near-zero net debt means EV ≈ market cap), against INR 2,501 Cr of EBIT — a 13.7% earnings yield. ROCE of 26.8% has been sustained for multiple years, demonstrating this is a structurally high-return asset, not a cyclical blip. The company's Urea-plus-agrochemicals model benefits from scale and long-established farmer relationships under the Uttam brand. The main reservation is regulatory: Indian fertiliser economics are ultimately set in New Delhi, and the government can compress margins when it suits policy goals. But the price you pay for this risk is genuinely low, and the balance sheet is now clean enough to fund growth entirely from internal cash flows.
